summary: Astrodrift is a web app that lets anyone type a spot in the sky and see what changed between NASA SPHEREx pictures of it. It fetches real SPHEREx cutouts from NASA's IRSA archive, lines up pictures of the same infrared colour from different six-month passes, and removes what stays fixed. What is left, such as a brown dwarf or other slow mover, shows up as a pair of spots: where it was, and where it is now. It also tracks a known moving object along its predicted path and reports honestly whether SPHEREx can detect it.
details:
Astrodrift: see what changed in the sky between NASA SPHEREx pictures.

What it does. SPHEREx photographs the whole sky about every six months, in 102 infrared colours. Because each picture is a different colour, two pictures cannot simply be laid over each other to look for change. Astrodrift solves that. The user picks a target or types right ascension and declination, and the app asks NASA's IRSA archive for SPHEREx cutouts of that patch. It groups the pictures by colour, lines them up on the same sky grid, removes the background, and matches brightness between passes so that fixed stars cancel out. Anything that moved or changed is left behind.

How it shows change. The app has six views of the same data:

- Flipbook: step through the real pictures one after another.

- Difference: subtract an earlier pass from a later one. Blue shows where something is brighter now and white shows where it was before.

- Layers: every pass painted in a different colour with fixed things removed.

- Stack: each pass as its own transparent layer, with its own on/off switch and opacity slider, coloured white, green and blue from oldest to newest.

- Colour: a false-colour infrared picture, clearly labelled as false colour.

- Follow: tracks a known moving object using its predicted path from JPL Horizons, centres every SPHEREx cutout on where the object should be at that picture's own time, stacks them, and measures a spectrum.

Mover finder. The Difference view lists only strong candidates: spots above a noise threshold that form a fainter-then-brighter pair a few pixels apart, that are not on a bright star or near the edge. If nothing qualifies, it says "No clear movers found" instead of listing noise.

Testing on a real object. I tested the Follow view on 2026 ED138, a dwarf planet candidate announced by the Vera C. Rubin Observatory. Across 76 SPHEREx pictures, the tool did not detect it (about 0.8 sigma against roughly 5 sigma needed). I report that result honestly: the object is too faint for these pictures. WISE 0855, a very cold brown dwarf, is the slow-mover test for the Difference view.

Limits. One SPHEREx pixel is about 6 arcseconds, so pictures are coarse. Crowded star fields create false candidates, and fast or faint movers can be missed. Candidates need follow-up checking before anyone calls them real.

What it is for. The aim is to make SPHEREx's repeated sky maps easy for students and amateur astronomers to explore, in the same spirit as the blink method that found Pluto.

Built with Python, Streamlit, Astropy, Astroquery, NumPy, SciPy, Plotly and Pillow. Code: https://github.com/ClarenceDG/astrodrift
